 Live .  29,042 viewing 29042 viewing Live page Updated 1 minute ago David Walliams accused of preying on girls as young as 15 after losing court battle to stop publication
 Summary
 Warning: This page contains distressing details. If you've been affected by this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line 
 David Walliams has been accused of preying on girls as young as 15 after he lost a court battle trying to block publication of the allegations
 In a joint report from ITV News and the Guardian , multiple women allege the comedian and author used his celebrity status to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women
 One girl claims she was 15 when Walliams first contacted her , and by the time she was 17 they were having sex - he strongly denies he groomed her
 Walliams denies all allegations, saying: "I am not a sexual predator." But he acknowledges "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people"
 The BBC says it's removing some content from its platforms - including his TV show Little Britain
 Walliams had asked the High Court to block the publication of the investigation , and said if the allegations were made public it was "highly likely" he would kill himself. The court refused the request, saying the risks could be mitigated
 The Metropolitan Police says it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News so "any potential victims" know how to report "any criminal allegations" - but it has not received any related reports of sexual assault or any other offences
 Close form Contact us
 Get in touch Media caption, "I think I was groomed, 100%," David Walliams accuser tells ITV News Live Reporting
 Edited by Alex Smith, Ben Hatton and Imogen James. Warning: This page contains graphic details
 Concerns over Walliams' behaviour on Britain's Got Talent, report alleges published at 18:23 GMT 18:23 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, David Walliams was a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent from 2012 to 2022
 While a judge on Britain's Got Talent, ITV News and the Guardian allege that there were
concerns from colleagues about Walliams’ behaviour.
 According to the reports, Walliams messaged a 19-year-old
colleague "you always put a smile on my face x", referred to her
as "gorgeous", and commented "hot" under an image of her and
others.
 It is claimed that she sent a screenshot of Walliams'
comments to colleagues, with the caption: "Erm, David’s comment on my insta of
us, WTF." 
 The Guardian reports that another insider on the show,
who was 24 when assigned to work with Walliams for a day in 2017, alleged he
stared at her chest in a way that made her feel uncomfortable.
 She recalled that she overheard Walliams describe her as "the one with the arse" and said she felt his behaviour was
"predatory" and made her feel "like I was not a person, but just
a body". 
 Walliams lawyers say he does not recall making this
remark, and denies staring at her chest or acting predatory, reports the
Guardian. 
 On the reports of his contact with the 19-year-old
colleague, Williams' lawyers say the Instagram comment was clearly meant as a
joke and that "gorgeous" was commonly used in the entertainment industry - adding that Walliams denies that he behaved inappropriately or harassed young women in the workplace.
 The show's production firm Fremantle UK has since said it is "disturbed and concerned" by the allegations made against Walliams

 David Walliams' career has not been without controversy published at 18:02 GMT 18:02 GMT 
 Chi Chi Izundu 
BBC News 
 Image source, Gianfranco Calcagno/FilmMagic Image caption, Walliams in character as Little Britain's Lou Todd in 2006
 In 2020, in the wake of Black Lives Matter protests, Walliams' BBC comedy sketch show Little Britain was removed from iPlayer. Walliams used black make-up and an afro wig to play a black woman. He and his comedy partner Matt Lucas both apologised saying they "regret that we played characters of other races". It returned in 2022 but with some scenes removed.
 In November 2022, the Guardian newspaper published a transcript of a recording of Walliams making what he described as "disrespectful comments" about two contestants whilst appearing as a judge on Britain's Got Talent (BGT). He apologised and left the show as a result. 
 He then took legal action in the High Court against Fremantle, the company behind ITV's BGT, alleging that they allowed his private comments to be leaked. The case was settled after both parties "reached an amicable resolution".
 His career as a children’s book author appeared to end last year, after the Telegraph published an article alleging Walliams had been accused of "harassing" junior employees at his publisher, Harper Collins UK, who confirmed they would not publish any more of his titles going forward.
 "To respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on internal matters," the company said.
 Walliams denied the allegations that he "behaved inappropriately".
 That same year, the BBC said a segment of the comedy panel show Would I Lie to You? wouldn't be broadcast after Walliams made two Nazi salutes during the Christmas special recording. The broadcaster said it was "completely unacceptable". 
 Walliams made the gestures during a segment in which a fellow panellist discussed a story about injuring their wrist while waving.

 Met Police says it has contacted Guardian and ITV published at 17:57 GMT 17:57 GMT 
 The Metropolitan Police says it contacted the Guardian and ITV last week to "ensure that any potential victims who they have spoken to could be made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police". 
 In a statement, the force says it has "not received any related reports of sexual assault or any other offences". 
 "Should we receive any reports, they will be carefully assessed. Anyone who contacts the police will be supported by specialist officers," it says.
 Walliams has denied the allegations made against him. 
 Responding to the Guardian and ITV investigation, he has said: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

 HarperCollins says it takes staff safety 'incredibly seriously' published at 17:20 GMT 17:20 GMT 
 David Walliams' former publisher HarperCollins UK has released a statement saying it takes staff safety "incredibly seriously". 
 As we mentioned earlier, the Guardian has reported claims that Walliams engaged in a consensual sexual relationship with an intern at the publisher in 2017, and that women in the office were reportedly warning about his behaviour. 
 A spokesperson for the publisher says: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams. 
 "We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."
 In late 2023, HarperCollins initiated an inquiry into Walliams, which wrapped up in 2024. He was then dropped from the publisher in December 2025, and in September this year HarperCollins said it would no longer publish his books.

 Waterstones looking to return unsold Walliams books to publisher published at 17:04 GMT 17:04 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Book retailer Waterstones says it will be returning the "small number of copies" it still has of Walliams' books to their publisher HarperCollins. 
 In a statement, the retailer says it was not aware of the allegations against Walliams, adding that he was dropped from the 2026 Waterstones Children's Book Festival as HarperCollins "withdrew [him] from events when they announced their decision not to publish any new titles with him".
 "HarperCollins also ceased supply of all David Walliams’ existing books, and we are in touch with them about returning to them the small number of copies which remain in stock in a few of our shops," it adds.

 Were social media users free to identify Walliams as the anonymous celebrity? published at 16:33 GMT 16:33 GMT 
 Dominic Casciani 
Home and legal correspondent 
 There is a massive practical issue concerning how far the writ of English law runs in cyber space.
 One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west" - which just underlines the concern among legal professionals.
 When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication.
 But the question is: how to enforce that? If a newspaper were to breach an order, the nature of a bona fide large media organisation’s audience means that publication is seen by judges to have a wide impact. 
 One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person is obviously less impactful. But that does not take into account the overall effect of thousands of people doing the same. 
 The Walliams case was complicated because his name and the media organisations he was seeking to gag were briefly published on a register of live cases when the case was filed. That register is not directly public - but the name somehow got out. Court officials later deleted it, as per other anonymity cases. 
 But that incident made some people think that they were free to reveal the identity of a seriously unwell man when, unless they were either lawyers or journalists trained in how reporting restrictions work, they may not have had a clue about the rules of anonymity.

 Government 'concerned' over use of injunctions - minister published at 15:38 GMT 15:38 GMT Breaking 
 Image source, House of Commons Image caption, Alex Davies-Jones says the government is "looking at what more" it can do on injunctions
 The government is "concerned" about the use of injunctions and is "looking at what more" it can do, justice minister Alex Davies-Jones tells the House of Commons. 
 It follows David Walliams unsuccessfully attempting to use the courts to block the Guardian and ITV News from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against him.

 Walliams messaged 18-year-old after she went to BGT show, report alleges published at 15:28 GMT 15:28 GMT 
 Noor Nanji 
Culture correspondent 
 The ITV and Guardian investigation also reports claims from a woman who is being called Sarah.
 She says she was 18 when she attended a Britain’s Got Talent show and sat behind the judges, including Walliams.
 According to the reports, Sarah says she was waiting for the train home when Walliams messaged her on Instagram. 
 He invited her and her friends to his hotel for something to eat the next day, it is alleged, and then to filming of the show.
 She says she went along, and afterwards they exchanged a few messages and he invited her to stay at his house in London, it is claimed.
 She says she agreed and went with a friend, but as they watched a film, he stroked her leg. He also followed her to the bathroom and tried to kiss her. She says she rejected his advances, the report says.
 Walliams told the investigation he did not force himself onto Sarah and denies there was any sexual contact with her. 
 He says both Sarah and her friend were "friendly" the next day and "did not raise any issue" with him.

 Did David Walliams have a right to appeal against court's decision? published at 15:06 GMT 15:06 GMT 
 Dominic Casciani 
Home and legal correspondent 
 Yes - but he did not exercise it. 
 When the High Court refused him his forever injunction - the judge naturally turned to the question of whether Walliams could challenge his ruling in the Court of Appeal. 
 That higher court doesn’t exist to give a claimant another go if they don’t agree with the outcome: there has to be a proper legal reason to appeal, such as if the judge made a serious mistake or had not followed a fair process. 
 Walliams’ legal team couldn’t give Mr Justice Nicklin last week an indication of what those grounds would be, saying in court that they had not been able to take instructions from their client because he was in hospital.
The judge, in fairness to Walliams, decided to grant him permission to appeal in principle - but on the proviso that he filed a proper challenge by 16:30 GMT yesterday.
That appeal - or alternatively a request for more time - was not filed. The BBC and others learned yesterday afternoon that Walliams had not filed his appeal. 
 So why didn’t we reveal his name? 
 The High Court had earlier ordered that if the deadline was passed with nothing from Walliams, ITN and the Guardian were free to publish - if they chose to do so - and only if they did go with their story would the rest of the media be able to identify that the comedian and author who had been fighting to remain anonymous.

 Britain's Got Talent production firm 'deeply disturbed' by allegations published at 15:00 GMT 15:00 GMT Breaking 
 Image source, PA Media Image caption, Walliams at a Britain's Got Talent event in 2020
 Britain's Got Talent production firm, Fremantle UK, says the company is "disturbed and concerned" by allegations made against former judge David Walliams. 
 Fremantle UK says "during his time on the show and in the intervening period, no complaint was ever made regarding his behaviour to Fremantle UK", adding he hasn't been a judge on the show for "more than four years".
 "If anyone feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone on any Fremantle or associated labels’ productions, we encourage them to come forward," a spokesperson says. 
 "We will treat any complaints seriously. Protecting the welfare of our employees, freelancers, contributors and fans has always been and absolutely remains paramount for the company," it adds.
 Walliams was a judge on the show for 10 series. He said his offer to appear in the 2023 series of the ITV show was withdrawn after the Guardian published disrespectful comments , external he made about two performers.

 'When I saw you at the Little Britain recording, I was enraptured' - alleged note from Walliams published at 14:53 GMT 14:53 GMT 
 One woman, a former model, alleges David Walliams groomed her as a teenager. She has waived her right to anonymity.
 Lilly Creightmore - who appeared on the TV show, Model Behaviour, when she was 16 - tells ITV she was 18 when Walliams first contacted her in 2003. He was 31.
 He had seen her with her mum at a Little Britain radio recording, the ITV report says. When Walliams later saw Lilly at a lingerie store event, he told her he had contacted Model Behaviour's production company and asked for her contact details, according to the investigation.
 The agency resisted initially, Lilly says, but he persisted, it is alleged.
 It is claimed Lilly then received a card from Walliams at her home address, which read:
 Quote Message When I saw you at the Little Britain recording, I was enraptured. Then when I saw you in Agent Provocateur, I so wanted to speak to you, but amongst all the frilly knickers I couldn’t find the words. I’d love to take you out sometime. I know we’ve never spoken but you seem lovely. David Walliams."
 A note allegedly sent by David Walliams to Lilly Creightmore in October 2003 
 Lilly was a vulnerable teenager, ITV reports, living either in foster care or her grandparents. When she was between homes and had nowhere to live, Walliams offered her his guest room.
 But according to the report, Lilly says there was no spare room. She slept on the sofa, but Walliams would ask her to stay in his bed every night, she alleges.
 "He definitely crossed the line physically in moments, when I was young, trying to coerce me into sleeping with him,” Lilly tells ITV. 
 "He would plead with me to share a bed with him and paw at me, trying to make me feel sorry for him."
 She reportedly says her refusal to have sex with Walliams sometimes made him angry, and he became rude to her. She ended up leaving and staying somewhere else.
 They kept in touch, on and off, for five years. Lilly says he invited her to Australia while on his Little Britain tour in 2007. When she said she'd go, but wasn't interested in anything romantic or sexual, Walliams "hit the roof", Lilly alleges.
 Lilly says he once messaged her saying: "You’re such a good friend, never going to the papers about me."
 According to ITV, Walliams says he does not remember messaging Lilly to tell her not to go to the papers and did not act inappropriately. He says he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".
 He says he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and feels "devastated" by her account. He denies the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

 BBC removing some content, including Little Britain, from platforms published at 14:45 GMT 14:45 GMT Breaking 
 The BBC says it is removing content, including Little Britain, after allegations about David Walliams' conduct. 
 A spokesperson for the BBC says: "These are serious allegations.
 "As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. 
 "We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is underway."

 Labour Party suspends Walliams as member published at 14:43 GMT 14:43 GMT Breaking 
 Henry Zeffman 
Chief political correspondent 
 The Labour Party has suspended the membership of David Walliams following today's allegations.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 David Walliams dropped by his agents published at 14:13 GMT 14:13 GMT Breaking 
 David Walliams has been dropped by his literary agents, Independent Talent Group. 
 A spokesperson for the company says: "ITG is deeply disturbed by the allegations concerning David Walliams. 
 "Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected. We are no longer representing him in any capacity."

 Women at HarperCollins warned others about Walliams' behaviour, report alleges published at 14:12 GMT 14:12 GMT 
 Walliams signed to publisher HarperCollins in 2008 and became one of the country's most successful children's writers. 
 In the Guardian's reporting, it is alleged that he began a consensual sexual relationship with an intern at the company, after meeting her in 2017. She was in her mid-20s, and he was 45.
 Around the office, women were reportedly warning about Walliams' behaviour, the report claims. 
 One woman says she went to HR after a young colleague showed her messages that Walliams had sent, asking her out. 
 Walliams' lawyers say that he messaged the woman at a time when he was "heartbroken and lonely" after his divorce. 
 In late 2023, HarperCollins initiated an inquiry into Walliams, which wrapped up in 2024. 
 He was dropped from the firm in December 2025, and in September 2026 it was announced HarperCollins would no longer publish his books.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Walliams: I behaved thoughtlessly at times but I am not a sexual predator published at 13:51 GMT 13:51 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Walliams pictured in 2023
 In response to the investigation by ITV and the Guardian, David Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
 "I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.
 "And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
 He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

 Walliams allegations come from joint ITV News and Guardian investigation published at 13:46 GMT 13:46 GMT 
 The allegations made against David Walliams come from a three-year joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian.
 You can read the ITV News report here , external , and t , external he Guardian report here. , external 
 As a reminder, Walliams was named after trying to block the publication of allegations against him - you can read our legal correspondent's analysis here.

 Walliams contacted 19-year-old model out of the blue, report alleges published at 13:35 GMT 13:35 GMT 
 Noor Nanji 
Culture correspondent 
 Another allegation in the Guardian and ITV investigation comes from a young woman who is being called Ella.
 Ella was a 19-year-old model when, she says, Walliams contacted her out of the blue and invited her for dinner.
 Unbeknown to her, the investigation alleges, Walliams had contacted her modelling agent and asked for her number. Lawyers say Walliams understood it had been provided with her knowledge and permission.
 After the call, Ella says she and Walliams went for dinner with other friends, and Walliams sent her a card and a bouquet of roses, and then invited her to a celebrity party at his home.
 Ella, who was by this time 20, says he took her on a tour of his house, and then tried to kiss her. She says she rejected his advances.
 She now calls what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".
 Walliams says he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He claims he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.
 Share close panel Share page Copy link About sharing 
 Walliams' lawyers tried to block publication on mental health grounds published at 13:12 GMT 13:12 GMT 
 Dominic Casciani 
Home and legal correspondent 
 David Walliams has been named because he had no legally sound reason to prevent the Guardian and ITN (which produces news for ITV) from disclosing their allegations, which he denies. 
His lawyers wanted the two organisations to be permanently gagged from running their story. They argued that if they were not stopped from running the claims, it would cause irreparable harm to Walliams’ mental health, potentially leading to him trying to take his own life. 
 That, they argued, would be a breach of the state’s duty, under the European Convention on Human Rights, to protect his right to life. 
Under that law, public bodies have a duty to take reasonable steps to try to preserve life, where they can do so. 
There’s no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it’s clear it had a responsibility to act. And this is why Walliams lost. 
 The responsibility to protect his life and help him get mentally better is on clinicians, not the court or the media. 
The bid to use human rights law to gag the media was exceptionally novel. Critically, the court did not say the allegations were true.
 That neutral position means Walliams, like anyone else who may feel unjustly maligned in the media, retains his right to try to sue for defamation or breach of privacy.

 Walliams first contacted 15-year-old girl on MySpace, report alleges published at 12:54 GMT 12:54 GMT 
 This post contains graphic details 
 Two women have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.
 The women are named as Alex and Jade by the Guardian and ITV, although they are not their real names.
 Alex alleges that she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15, and handed him some scripts she had written as she wanted to be a comedy writer. 
 Alex says that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years. They were having sex by 2006, when she was 17, the report alleges.
 The Guardian reports her as saying when she thinks about her experiences "it's like a trauma response".
 Jade also alleges she met Walliams when she was 15, in the summer of 2007. After he sent her a private message on MySpace, she says, they met in a cafe. 
 "It wasn’t long until he asked me if I’d ever had sex before," the Guardian reports her as saying. 
 After leaving the cafe, she alleges that Walliams kissed her on a side street and then invited her back to his house. At his home she says he kissed her and lifted up her T-shirt. 
 "I wasn't ready for sex... I didn't want to be touched in that way at all. I mean, I was only a 15-year-old," Jade tells the Guardian. 
 Lawyers for Walliams deny he groomed Alex, and deny him having had any sexual contact with Jade.
